in the revised manuscript). These results further demonstrate that DS2 is a direct
downstream target of HER1.
3. The authors identified six haplotypes of HER1 in a natural cultivated rice
accessions, and showed that accessions with Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 exhibited longer
stigma length than those with Hap1 in Supplementary Fig. 8c, how do these compare
to those with Hap5 and Hap6? Additionally, the authors should further examine both
the expression and H3K9me2 levels of DS2 among accessions with different
haplotypes, this result would provide very strong evidence to confirm the conclusion
of this study.
Response: We apologize for the misunderstanding created for you. In the revised
manuscript, we have provided a clearer description of the phenotypic differences
among Hap1-6: “Only the accessions with Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 showed an increase
in total stigma length compared to those carrying Hap1, while no significant
differences were observed for other haplotypes.” (Line 294-296, Page 10 in the
revised manuscript)
Following your suggestion, we selected three accessions from each of Hap1-Hap4,
which had shown statistically significant phenotypic differences, and performed
qPCR analysis of DS2 in their stigmas. Only one accession, W108 (carrying Hap2),
showed decreased expression compared to the three specific accessions, C069
(carrying Hap2), W259 (carrying Hap3), and W272 (carrying Hap3), while no
significant differences were observed among others (Supplementary Fig. 11g in the
revised manuscript). This differential expression did not show a clear association
with the phenotype. Furthermore, we found that the variation explained by haplotypes
was less than the variation explained by subpopulations (Supplementary Table 3 in
the revised manuscript). This lack of correlation between HER1 haplotypes, DS2
expression, and phenotypes has strengthened our hypothesis that the increased total
stigma length observed in accessions with Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 may be caused by
differences in subpopulation genetic architecture, rather than natural variations in
HER1.
4. Stigma exsertion is considered to be a key trait in determining domestication of O.
rufipogon into the Asian cultivated rice. In general, O. rufipogon, indica and japonica
have highest, moderate and lowest level of stigma exsertion, respectively. In this study,
the authors found that accessions with Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 (almost indica varieties)
have longer stigma than those with Hap1, Hap5, and Hap6 (predominantly found in
japonica and aus varieties). Thus, it will be of great interest to explore the genetic
variations of HER1 in wild rice and examine how different haplotype have been
artificially selected during rice domestication process.
Response: We had analyzed the nucleotide diversity (π) of HER1 and its flanking
regions (50 kb upstream and 50 kb downstream) in both cultivated rice (Oryza sativa)
and wild rice (Oryza rufipogon). Compared to the flanking regions, HER1 exhibits
notably low nucleotide diversity in both cultivated and wild populations
(Supplementary Fig. 11h in the revised manuscript). This suggests that the
minimal natural variation in the locus of HER1 might be the result of natural selection
rather than artificial selection. This is also the reason we employed the mutant allele
in her1 rather than natural variations of HER1 for our breeding applications.
Minor points
1. Null mutation of HER1 could not only increase rice stigma exsertion, but also lead
to detrimental effects, such as reduced grain size and seed setting rate. It needs
concern with regarding the potential impact of utilization of her1 allele on the final
yield of hybrid rice.
Response: We strongly agree with you that the final yield of hybrid rice must be tested.
To address this concern, six hybrid rice combinations were developed by crossing the
male sterile lines II-32A and herA with three restorer lines, Shuhui12, Shuhui527, and
Fuhui838 (Supplementary Fig. 13a in the revised manuscript). The hybrid rice
combinations developed using herA and those using II-32A showed no significant
differences in plant height, panicle number per plant, panicle length, grain number per
panicle, seed setting rate, thousand-grain weight, and yield per plant (Supplementary
Fig. 13b-h in the revised manuscript). We also tested the final yield of every field
plot and found that none of them revealed significant differences between the hybrid
rice combinations developed using herA and those using II-32A (Supplementary Fig.
13i in the revised manuscript). These results confirmed that the negative effects of
her1 may be masked by the dominant allele from the restorer line in the hybrid
generation (F ) and indicated the significant practical value of HER1 in hybrid rice
1
production.
2. To make the result clearer in Fig.3a, it is better to label the fold change of histone
lysine methylation levels in her1 compared to II-32B in each panel.
Response: Following your suggestion, we have labeled the fold changes in each panel
of Fig. 3a in the revised manuscript. This modification provides clearer information
about changes in methylation levels observed in our experiment.
3. The molecular function of DS and its regulatory role in pistil development have not
been investigated in this study. Alternatively, the authors could make some reasonable
speculations in the Discussion.
Response: Following your suggestion, we have added reasonable speculations on the
molecular function of DS2 and its regulatory role in pistil development in the
Discussion (Line 392-399, Page 14 in the revised manuscript).
4. The authors claim that introducing her1 allele into II-32A could increase its hybrid
seed production by more than 20%. Actually, in this study, this result was obtained
from an outcrossing test of herA and the maintainer line, but not the restored line.
Response: Thanks for your insightful comment. The outcrossing between male sterile
lines and maintainer lines represents an essential reproductive process in hybrid rice
seed production. We specifically chose the maintainer line as the male parent in our
experiments because restorer lines typically have longer growth periods compared to
male sterile/maintainer lines, and these differences can fluctuate substantially
depending on environmental conditions. By using the maintainer line, we ensured
synchronized flowering periods between two parents, which was critical for the
reliability and reproducibility of our experimental results.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Although there have been some reports on the cloning of rice stigma exsertion genes,
such as the major effect genes GS3 and GW5 for grain shape, there has been no field
experiment to confirm whether these genes can increase hybrid seed yield. In this
study, the authors cloned a new gene HER1 that controls rice stigma morphology and
exsertion, and found that its loss-of-function allele her1 significantly increased the
stigma exsertion rate, outcrossing rate, and hybrid seed yield. In addition, the authors
also revealed the epigenetic regulatory mechanism of HER1 affecting rice stigma
exsertion and created corresponding genetic materials to confirm it. Undoubtedly, this
is an innovative and very meaningful work that will help further increase hybrid rice
yield and ensure food security. However, there are still a few minor shortcomings that
I hope the authors can improve further.
Response: Thanks for your insightful comments, which have significantly improved
our manuscript and enabled us to present more convincing results. We have addressed
these specific comments in detail below.
1. Line127-129: Why was LOC_Os02g47900 directly identified as the only candidate
gene? There is no reasonable explanation.
Response: We apologize for our insufficient description. Regarding
LOC_Os02g47900, we have provided a more comprehensive description for why it
has been chosen as the candidate gene (Line 154-156, Page 6 in the revised
manuscript).
2. Line131-134: Regarding the domain structure of the HER1 encoded protein, the
authors should explain clearly how the protein domain structure was obtained here in
the text or in the Materials and Methods section, such as the website or software used.
Response: The details about the website used for protein domain structure analysis
have been included in the Methods section (Line 507-508, Page 18 in the revised
manuscript).
3. In Fig. 4g, Up-regulated DEGs ?
Response: Thank you for pointing out this error. We did utilize a subset of genes that
were up-regulated in the her1 mutant, as the mutation of HER1 enhanced the
expression of a series of genes. But there was a clear error in the description in the
main text. We have corrected this content and added more detailed descriptions to
avoid any misunderstanding (Line 259-260, Page 9 in the revised manuscript).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors described an EMS screen in which they identified HER1 gene as
putatively implicated in regulating stigma size and exsertion. Further analyses of 2
CRISPR-Cas9 derived KO of HER1 gene, as well as its functional complementation
confirmed the implication of HER1 protein in the stigma size and exsertion.
Importantly, HER1 roles was confirmed both in indica and japonica.
The authors then demonstrate that HER1 is a histone methyltransferase that
specifically binds and methylate H3 at position K9. The genomic approach then
demonstrate that decreased H3K9me2 deposition is observed throughout the genome
in the her1 ko, and is accompanied by several hundreds of DEG. A cross-analyses of
the genomic data in fine identified 5 putative targets in the stigma, including DS2
gene. They finally confirmed the potential target gene DS2 in stigma size and
exsertion, as well as the potential agronomical impact of their discovery on hybrid
seed production.
It's a well-crafted, easy-to-read story with a potentially interesting impact on
agronomy. However, several points need to be better addressed to consider this story
sufficiently complete.
Response: Thanks for your insightful comments, which have significantly improved
our manuscript and enabled us to present more convincing results. We have addressed
these specific comments in detail below.
1. A description of the known role of SDG706 or their homolog is missing. SDG706
correspond to SUVR5 in Arabidopsis thaliana (see and cite doi:
10.1016/j.bbaexp.2007.04.003) that was already described to alter the expression of a
subset of stimulus response genes and modify H3K9me2 (PLoS Genet
2012;8(10):e1002995. doi: 10.1371/journal.pgen.1002995) .These informations
should be present in the MS, at least in the discussion.
Response: Following your advice, we have added a description of SUVR5 in
Arabidopsis thaliana in both Introduction and Discussion sections (Lines 88-89, Page
3-4, and Lines 374-377, Page 13 in the revised manuscript), including citations to
the suggested literature. Additionally, we gave a brief description of the roles of
histone modifications and H3K9 methylation in the Introduction section (Lines 69-92,
Page 3-4 in the revised manuscript).
2. In A. thaliana, SUVR5 is regulating gene expression and H3K9me2 deposition in a
DNA methylation independent manner. Is it also true for SDG706 in rice? To confirm
this point, a global DNA methylation analyses should be performed in II-32B, her1
and potentially also in the HER1 over-expressing line. This is an important question
because the decoupling of histone modifications and methylation is not so common.
Response: We appreciate your insightful suggestion. Following this recommendation,
we performed Whole Genome Bisulfite Sequencing (WGBS) on stigmas from both
wild-type (II-32B) and the her1 mutant. In contrast to neighboring genes
(LOC_Os03g02450 and LOC_Os03g02470), the DS2 gene region exhibits very low
levels of DNA methylation, while these neighboring genes show considerable
enrichment of CG, CHG, and CHH methylation in both wild-type and her1 (Fig. R1).
Importantly, we did not observe significant differences in DNA methylation patterns
at the DS2 locus between wild-type and her1, despite the clear differences in
H3K9me2 levels and DS2 expression (Fig. 4h, i in the revised manuscript). These
observations strongly suggest that HER1 regulates H3K9me2 and DS2 expression in a
DNA methylation-independent manner, similar to what has been reported for SUVR5
in Arabidopsis.
Fig. R1 | WGBS analysis on stigmas from II-32B and her1. Genome browser tracks
showing CG, CHG, and CHH methylation enrichment on DS2 and its neighboring
gene regions in both II-32B and her1.
3. IF DS2 gene is an key target of HER1 HKMT, then
> its over expression may mimic her1 phenotype,
> DS2 expression should be lower in overexpression line of HER1,
> a double mutant her1 and ds2 should have the same phenotype than ds2 ko alone
The authors should test all 3 hypotheses
Response: Following your advice, we knocked out DS2 in the her1 mutant, while also
overexpressing DS2 in the wild-type II-32B. The her1-ds2 double mutant exhibited a
significant reduction in both stigma length and width, indicating that the
functional loss of DS2 restricts the biological effects of her1 in regulating stigma size
(Fig. 5e-g in the revised manuscript). Overexpression lines of DS2 showed
significantly increased stigma length and exsertion rate, similar to her1 (Fig. 5a-d in
the revised manuscript). These new results strengthen our conclusion that HER1
targets DS2 and regulates its transcription level, ultimately influencing stigma
exsertion.
The HER1 overexpression lines showed no significant change in stigma morphology
and exsertion rate, as well as expression of DS2 compared to the wild-type
(Supplementary Fig. 5e-i in the revised manuscript, and Fig. R2 below).
Therefore, we propose that rice plants might be insensitive to changes in HER1
transcriptional levels, with phenotypic variation occurring only when HER1 is
functionally compromised.
Fig. R2 | Relative expression of DS2 in the overexpression lines of HER1.
OsActin1 was used as the internal control. The data are presented as means ± s.d. P
values above the bars were calculated using one-way ANOVA.
4. 35S promoter is often targeted by silencing mechanisms. Therefore, KO and over
expression line of HER1 gene should be validated using the native HER1 antibody
used for the Cut&Tag approach.
Response: We concur with your concerns regarding the 35S promoter, and have
therefore employed the ubiquitin promoter to drive HER1 overexpression. The new
results are now presented in the revised manuscript, replacing the original 35S-related
content (Line 182-186, Page 7 and Supplementary Fig. 5e-i in the revised
manuscript). Following the reviewer's advice, we have validated these
overexpression lines using Western Blot analysis, confirming the accumulation of
GFP-HER1 protein in the transgenic plants (Supplementary Fig. 3e in the revised
manuscript). Importantly, the ubiquitin-driven HER1 overexpression plants still
exhibited stigma phenotypes very similar to the wild-type, which further substantiates
our hypothesis as described previously.
5. The exact role of H3K9me2 to understand its function in DS2 expression is missing.
Indeed, cut&tag and RNA-seq analyses where performed on fresh stigma, where DS2
is specifically expressed. Although DS2 locus is targeted by HER1, that also
potentially deposit H3K9me2 along the promoter and the gene body of DS2, DS2
remains quite highly expressed in the stigma. this observation is counter-intuitive
since H3K9me2 is supposed to drastically reduce the expression of the targeted gene.
Majority of H3K9me2 methylation is realized by SUVH-type HKMT, mainly on
repeated sequences such as Transposable Elements, satellites repeats and inactive
ribosomal RNA genes. In that context, the authors should better discuss this aspect
and consider the implication of HER1 binding activity, potentially independently on
its capacity to deposit H3K9me2. In the Fig2, the authors prepared a HER1-CP1 line
and successfully complemented the mutation. By doing a directed mutation of HER-
CP1 at the active site of the SET domain, the authors will be able to demonstrate (1)
whether the SET activity is required to complement the phenotype, and (2) whether
HER1 with a mutated active site still accumulate at DS2 locus in the stigma (even just
by ChIP-qPCR).
This approach would allow to better characterize the role HER1 as a histone modifier
and/or reader.
Response: We appreciate your insightful observation regarding the seemingly counter-
intuitive relationship between H3K9me2 marks and DS2 expression. Gene expression
is regulated by a complex interplay of multiple epigenetic and transcriptional factors
rather than H3K9me2 alone. Additionally, H3K9me2 modulates gene expression
rather than completely silencing it in all contexts. In other words, H3K9me2 functions
as a fine-tuning regulator rather than a binary on/off switch. The stigma-specific
expression of DS2 likely results from a balance between repressive histone marks
(such as H3K9me2) and strong tissue-specific transcriptional activators binding to its
promoter region. In the her1 mutant, the reduction of H3K9me2 on the DS2 promoter
and gene body may disrupt this finely-tuned balance, allowing for the enhanced
expression of DS2 beyond its normal levels.
The mutated HER1 protein in the her1 mutant lacks the SET domain, which has been
confirmed to be the histone-binding site of HER1 (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 8
in the revised manuscript). Therefore, we performed ChIP-qPCR assays in both
wild-type II-32B and her1 using the α-HER1 antibody. The enrichment of HER1 on
multiple sites in the DS2 gene region was significantly decreased in the her1 mutant
compared to the wild-type (Supplementary Fig. 10b, c in the revised manuscript).
These results demonstrate that HER1 with a mutated active site fails to accumulate at
the DS2 locus, further indicating the regulatory effect of HER1 on DS2.
6. Better explain the sigles along the MS (-line 48: What means GS3 sigle ?; -line 53:
What means GW5 sigle ?; -line 66: :What means HER1 sigle?; -line 70: What mean
DS2 sigle?)
Response: We have revised the manuscript to provide the full names of all gene
symbols when they first appear (Line 50-55, Page 2, Line 61 -62, Page 3, and Line
93-99, Page 4).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Liao et al., provide a important stigma exsertion mutants in rice. Her1 encoded a SET
domain protein, which might be involved in histone H3K9me2 and increasing the
transcripts of DS2. The mutant phenotype is important for hybrid breeding. The
results is potentially interesting in epigenetic field, rice hybrid breeding field, and
stigma development field.
Response: Thanks for your insightful comments, which have significantly improved
our manuscript and enabled us to present more convincing results. We have addressed
these specific comments in detail below.
Major concerns:
1) The most of concerns of the function of HER1. HER1, SDG706, which is a
homology of SUVR5 and It probably not contains very low KMT activity. The
western blot might be not sensitive enough. The mass spectrometry and radio activity
of SAM might provide the new results. Otherwise, we don’t the real biochemical
function of HER1.
Response: We appreciate your suggestion. The in vitro methyltransferase activity of
HER1/SDG706 was also tested by a previous study (Ding et al., Plant Sci., 2007,
10.1016/j.plantsci.2007.03.009) which had been cited in our manuscript (Line 213,
Page 8). They used radioactive isotope-labeled SAM to conduct in vitro enzyme
activity assays and likewise failed to detect methyltransferase activity for
HER1/SDG706. The consistency between our findings and this independent study
using a highly sensitive detection method further validates the reliability of our
experimental results.
2) There are many homologies of HER1 in rice, the only mutation of SUVR
subfamily might be not enough to see any reduction of H3K9me2. In Arabidopsis,
SUVH subfamily is much important than SUVR subfamily in H3K9me2. Therefore,
the replicates of western blot and negative controls are necessary.
Response: We agree with your concern and have addressed it by performing two
additional biological replicates in both wild-type II-32B and the her1 mutant. These
new experiments consistently confirmed our previous finding that her1 exhibits a
notable decrease in global H3K9me2 levels compared to the wild-type (Fig. R3). This
reproducible result strengthens our conclusion regarding HER1's role in H3K9
methylation regulation.
Fig. R3 | Immunoblotting analysis on H3K9me2 in stigmas of wild-type II-32B
and the her1 mutant. The numbers represent the fold changes of her1 compared to
WT, with H3 as control.
3)Besides pre-SET, SET, and post SET domain, HER1 harbor C2H2 zinc figure
domain. We wonder how HER1 bound to H3K9me1, H3K9me2, and H3K9me3. ITC
might help us to answer these questions. Generally, pre-SET, SET, and post SET
domain did not show any binding activity to H3K9me1, H3K9me2, and H3K9me3.
Response: We strongly agree with you that binding site of HER1 to H3K9me must be
investigated. We divided the HER1 protein into three parts, HER1-P1, HER1-P2, and
HER1-P3 (P3 contains pre-SET, SET, and post-SET domains), and performed peptide
pull-down assays with H3K9me1/2/3 peptides to test the binding region of HER1
(Supplementary Fig. 8a in the revised manuscript). Among the three fragments,
only HER1-P3, which encompasses the entire SET domain architecture, demonstrated
binding affinity to H3K9me peptides (Supplementary Fig. 8b in the revised
manuscript). These results are consistent with our pull-down experiments using
HER1-1-624, which is encoded by the coding sequence from her1 mutant that lacks
the SET domain, resulting in its inability to bind to H3K9me (Fig. 3f in the revised
manuscript). This series of results clearly demonstrates that HER1 interacts with
H3K9me through its SET domain and regulates H3K9me2 levels.
4) Generally, H3K9me2 is located in the heterochromatin, but not in euchromatin. It’s
hard to understand analysis of transcription with H3K9me2 and HER1 target. Therefore,
the upregulation of DS2 might be second effector, not direct effector by HER1.
In another word, the upregulated DS2 might be not caused by the downregulation of
H3K9me in her1 plants.
Response: Although H3K9 is mainly localized in heterochromatin, studies have
demonstrated that H3K9 is involved in regulation of gene expression. For instance,
SUVR5 functions as an H3K9 methyltransferase, modifying H3K9me2 levels and
controlling a subset of genes involved in environmental stress responses and pathogen
defense (Elena et al., PLos Genet., 2012, 10.1371/journal.pgen.1002995).
Additionally, our Cut&Tag and ChIP analyses indeed indicate that HER1 is enriched
at numerous gene loci, and its impact on transcriptional levels is evident, which is also
consistent with changes in H3K9me2 levels (Fig. 4, and Supplementary Fig. 10b, c
in the revised manuscript). Therefore, we still believe that the upregulation of DS2
was the direct effect caused by mutation in HER1.
5) We wonder whether HER1 specifically bind to the DS2 and fulfill the H3K9me2 at
this locus. The genetic evidence between HER1 and DS2 is necessary.
Response: Following your suggestion, we knocked out DS2 in the her1 mutant, while
also overexpressing DS2 in the wild-type II-32B. The her1-ds2 double mutant
exhibited a significant reduction in both stigma length and width, indicating that the
functional loss of DS2 restricts the biological effects of her1 in regulating stigma size
(Fig. 5e-g 11 in the revised manuscript). Overexpression lines of DS2 showed
significantly increased stigma length and exsertion rate, similar to her1 (Fig. 5a-d in
the revised manuscript). These new results strengthen our conclusion that HER1
targets DS2 and regulates its transcription level, ultimately influencing stigma
exsertion.
6) The correlation analysis of the biological replicates of Cut&Tag and RNA seq are
required in supplemental Figures. Otherwise, we don’t know the real quality.
Response: Following your suggestion, we performed PCA analysis on data from both
Cut&Tag-seq and RNA-seq and confirmed the consistency between biological
replicates (Supplementary Fig. 9 in the revised manuscript).
Minor concerns:
1) The biological functions of H3K9 in mammalian and plants are necessary in
introduction section.
Response: Following your advice, we gave a brief description of the roles of
histone modifications and H3K9 methylation in the Introduction section (Lines 69-92,
Page 3-4 in the revised manuscript).
2) The functions of DS2 is also needed in introduction.
Response: We appreciate your suggestion. DS2 encodes an SDR family protein with
unknown function. SDRs constitute a super family of proteins that are involved in
various biosynthetic and metabolic pathways in plants. Since we have limited
experimental evidence on its precise function at this stage, we believe it is more
appropriate to present our speculations about its function and its potential
involvement in metabolic pathways in the Discussion section rather than the
Introduction (Line 392-399, Page 14 in the revised manuscript).
3) The structure of HER1 and the phylogenetic tree of HER1 are necessary.
Response: Following your suggestion, we presented the phylogenetic tree of HER1 in
the revised manuscript and clarified the homologous relationship between HER1 and
Arabidopsis SUVR5 (Line 194-199, Page 7, and Supplementary Fig. 6 in the
revised manuscript). Additionally, we further elaborated on the reported functions of
SUVR5, both in the Introduction and Discussion sections (Line 88-91, Page 3-4, and
Line 374-377, Page 13 in the revised manuscript).

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In the revised manuscript, the authors have addressed the feedback provided by the
reviewer, and their responses are deemed satisfactory. I have no further comments.

which significantly improved the clarity and rigor of our work. Thank you for your
careful review.

The author answered my questions, please accept.

comments helped clarify the text, fix issues, and strengthen the scientific soundness of
the work. We appreciate your time and support.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I am satisfied with the answers given by the authors and agree that this revised
version provides evidence that seems to validate the stated hypotheses. I would just
remind the authors to also deposit the WGBS data in order to make them publicly
accessible.
Response: Thank you very much for your supportive evaluation. We are glad the
revision resolves your comments and more clearly supports the hypotheses. As you
advised, we are currently depositing the WGBS data in the SRA database and will
make them openly accessible before publication; the accession number will be added
to the Data Availability section at the proof stage.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
1) Although the authors put the genetic relationship between HER1 and DS2 in this
version. The biological function of HER1 remain unclear, especially for functions of
HER1 in histone methylation. Based on western blot and ChIP-seq told the authors
that H3K9me2 was reduced in her1, but did not suggest that HER1 is histone
methyltransferase for H3K9me2.
Based on western blot (Figure 3A), we observed that H3K36me1, H3K36me2,
H3K9me1, and H3K9me2 were reduced in her1. Therefore, the reduction in
H3K9me2 might be the secondary effector by mutations in HER1. The in vitro
histone methyltransferase assay using mass spectrometry and radio activity of SAM is
necessary. In this version, the author did not provide these important results, and the
conclusion based on histone modification need more evidence. Again, Line 208
“These results indicate that HER1 protein regulates H3K9me2 levels in plants”, the
evidence is not enough, based on the reduction of 3K36me1, H3K36me2, H3K9me1,
and H3K9me2 in her1.
Response: Thank you again for your thoughtful review and insightful suggestions
regarding the biological function of HER1 and the evidence for its role in histone
methylation regulation.
The in vitro methyltransferase activity of HER1/SDG706 was previously tested by
Ding et al. (Plant Sci., 2007, 10.1016/j.plantsci.2007.03.009), which has been cited in
our manuscript (Line 213, Page 8). Using radioactive isotope-labeled SAM, they also
failed to detect direct methyltransferase activity for HER1/SDG706 (Fig. R1). The
consistency between our findings (Fig. 3c) and this independent study using a highly
sensitive detection method validates the reliability of our experimental approach.
The functional similarity between HER1 and its characterized homolog SUVR5,
which catalyzes H3K9me2 independent of DNA methylation, supports our findings.
Although HER1 does not exhibit direct methyltransferase activity in vitro, it may
regulate H3K9me2 through alternative mechanisms such as histone
binding/maintenance, or serving as a regulatory component of methyltransferase
complexes, as discussed in our manuscript (Discussion Section).
Furthermore, our Cut&Tag analysis provides compelling evidence for direct
chromatin regulation. The Venn diagram (Fig. 4e) reveals substantial overlap between
HER1 binding sites and H3K9me2-marked regions, with 57% of HER1 peaks co-
localizing with H3K9me2 peaks. This high degree of spatial co-localization indicates
direct chromatin binding rather than indirect downstream effects.
Collectively, these findings strongly demonstrate that HER1 plays a direct role in
H3K9me2 regulation rather than acting solely through secondary mechanisms.
We acknowledge that multiple histone modifications are reduced in her1, such as
H3K36me1, H3K36me2, and H3K9me1. These changes likely represent secondary
consequences resulting from the disruption of H3K9me2-mediated chromatin
structure rather than direct effects of HER1. While these aspects are intriguing, the
detailed investigation of these potential secondary effects is beyond the scope of the

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Hybrid rice has achieved a significant leap in rice yield, but the low outcrossing rate of sterile lines limits hybrid seed production due to rice’s self-pollinating habits, constraining the further development and widespread adoption of hybrid rice. Stigma exsertion is a critical trait affecting outcrossing rate. Here we characterize a rice mutant, high exsertion rate 1 (her1), characterized by enlarged stigma and enhanced stigma exsertion. HER1 encodes a SET domain-containing protein that binds to histone H3 at methylated lysine 9 and regulates H3K9me2 levels. Loss of function of HER1 results in reduced H3K9me2 levels in her1, increasing the transcription of Downstream 2 (DS2), which positively controls stigma size. Using the loss-of-function allele of her1, we develop a high-exsertion male-sterile line herA, which increases hybrid seed production by more than 20% in field conditions, substantiating the breeding value of HER1 in hybrid seed production.

---

## Introduction

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is a highly self-pollinating crop with flowering traits that favor self-pollination over cross-pollination1. However, hybrid rice seeds are produced when the female parent (male-sterile line) receives pollen from the male parent (restorer line) and undergoes fertilization2. Therefore, the outcrossing rate of the sterile line critically limits hybrid seed production. The outcrossing rate of rice is influenced by both environmental and genetic factors. The environmental effects can be optimized through cultivation techniques3. Genetic factors associated with plant morphology, flowering habits, and the structures of floral organs are all closely related to outcrossing. Stigma size and exsertion rate are key traits determining the outcrossing rate4.

Research on the rice OsPINOID (OsPID) gene has provided some insight into rice stigma formation. Initially discovered in Arabidopsis, PINOID (PID) encodes a serine-threonine protein kinase involved in polar auxin transport5,6. In rice, the reduced function of OsPID results in the absence or diminutive size of stigmas, while its overexpression leads to excessive stigma proliferation, forming up to three or even four stigmas in a single floret, accompanied by a reduced number of stamens7,8. Defective Stigma and Panicle (DSP) encodes an AP2/ERF-domain transcription factor that directly binds to the promoter of OsPID and regulates its transcription levels, influencing rice stigma differentiation9.

Numerous quantitative trait loci (QTL) controlling stigma exsertion have been identified, but only a few genes have been cloned10–20. Grain Size 3 (GS3) is a major gene that controls grain length in rice21,22, and is also the first gene cloned to regulate stigma exsertion. The loss-of-function allele of GS3 not only increases grain length but also elongates the style, making the stigma more likely to extend outside the spikelet, ultimately leading to a significant increase in exsertion rate11. Through a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on 533 accessions, two genes, GS3 and Grain Width 5 (GW5), associated with stigma exsertion were identified23. GW5 encodes a calmodulin-binding protein and acts as a negative regulator of grain width24. The strong functional allele of GW5 can reduce spikelet width, making it easier for stigmas to extend outside the glumes. The haplotype combination GW5gs3 can significantly enhance stigma exsertion as well as the appearance quality of rice grains23. Based on the correlation between grain shape and stigma exsertion, three genes regulating grain size, GS3, Grain Width 8 (GW8), and Grain Shape 9 (GS9), were chosen, and their single and multiple mutant lines were constructed25. Loss of function of these three genes leads to narrower or longer grains21,26,27 and single mutants of all three genes showed enhanced stigma exsertion, an effect that was more pronounced in the double and triple mutants. The outcrossing rate and grain length-to-width ratio of the triple mutant lines were significantly improved25. However, the effects of these genes on enhancing hybrid seed production have not been tested under field conditions.

Epigenetics plays a crucial role in regulating plant growth and development, with histone modification being one of the most critical mechanisms in this regulatory system28. Histone modifications primarily include methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation, and ubiquitination, which are closely associated with gene expression, DNA damage repair and recombination29. The establishment of histone methylation primarily depends on SET domain-containing proteins, which catalyze the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to target lysine residues on histones30. These proteins can be classified into several subfamilies based on their structural characteristics and functions, including SET1, SET2, SU(VAR) 3-9, EZH, and SMYD, among others, which specifically regulate histone methylation modifications at different lysine residues31. H3K9 methylation, especially H3K9me2, is a highly prevalent repressive histone mark in plants and plays crucial roles in maintaining genome stability, regulating transposon activity and controlling gene expression32,33. In Arabidopsis thaliana, the SU(VAR) 3-9 homologs (SUVHs) and SU(VAR) 3-9 related proteins (SUVRs) constitute two important subfamilies of SET domain proteins, which play crucial roles in the establishment of histone H3K9 methylation34. SUVHs possess a unique SRA domain, which is associated with their function to specifically recognize DNA methylation and catalyze histone methylation. For example, SUVH4, also known as KRYPTONITE (KYP), binds to methylated DNA CHG/CHH sites to establish H3K9me235. Unlike SUVHs, SUVR5 has been demonstrated to catalyze H3K9me2 independent of DNA methylation, contributing to repressing gene expression36. H3K9 methylation is closely associated with various important traits in plants, including stress responses and flowering time, among others37–40. However, there are currently no research reports on its relationship with stigma development and stigma exsertion.

Here, we report a gene, High Exsertion Rate 1 (HER1), that regulates stigma exsertion by directly controlling the stigma size, which acts differently from those genes that regulate grain shape. HER1 encodes a SET domain-containing protein that is homologous to SUVR5 in Arabidopsis thaliana. HER1 specifically binds to histone H3 at methylated lysine 9 and regulates H3K9me2 levels. Loss of function of HER1 leads to a reduction in H3K9me2 levels, increasing the transcription of the downstream target, Downstream 2 (DS2), and expanding stigma size. Using the loss-of-function allele of HER1, we develop a high-exsertion male-sterile line herA, which can increase hybrid seed production by more than 20% in field conditions, substantiating the breeding value of HER1 in improving hybrid seed production.

---

## Results

Mutant her1 showed enlarged stigma and increased stigma exsertion rate
We utilized ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenesis on the indica three-line hybrid rice maintainer II-32B, which shows purple-black stigmas, and obtained a mutant with a high stigma exsertion rate, her1. Compared to the wild-type II-32B, the stigma exsertion rate of her1 significantly increased from 36.32% to 70.63%, an increase of 94.47% (Fig. 1a, c). Microscopic measurements of pistils revealed that the overall size of the pistil in her1 was larger than that of the wild-type (Fig. 1b). Specifically, the stigma length (brush-like part) increased from 0.96 mm to 1.25 mm, the stigma width (brush-like part) increased from 0.35 mm to 0.45 mm, and the style length (non-brush-like part) increased from 0.78 mm to 0.87 mm (Fig. 1d–f). Stigma exsertion is a key factor in determining the outcrossing rate and hybrid seed production. In her1, the stigma exsertion rate was significantly increased by nearly 100% compared to the wild-type, suggesting that the gene controlling this mutant trait could have high breeding value.

To evaluate the impact of gene mutation on the growth and development of her1 plants, we conducted agronomic trait assessments on both wild-type II-32B and her1. Compared to the wild-type, the grain size of her1 was slightly smaller, with grain length reduced by 0.16 mm (1.88%) and grain width reduced by 0.07 mm (2.02%) (Fig. 1g–i). But the ratio of grain length to width remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 1a). The seed setting rate of her1 decreased from 78.48% to 71.29% (Supplementary Fig. 1b). However, there were no significant differences in panicle number per plant (tiller number), panicle length, and grain number per panicle between her1 and the wild-type (Supplementary Fig. 1c–e). The reduction in grain size resulted in a 1.35 g (5.33%) decrease in the thousand-grain weight of her1 (Supplementary Fig. 1f). Potassium iodide staining was used to investigate whether the change in the seed setting rate of her1 was related to its pollen fertility, but there was no significant difference between II-32B and her1 (Supplementary Fig. 2).

To further explore the stigma trait variations in her1, we observed the stigmas of both wild-type and her1 using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The density and thickness of stigma brushes in her1 were increased compared to the wild-type, and the stigma of her1 appeared overall more robust and substantial (Fig. 1j, k). In the style, the epidermal cells of her1 showed notable protrusions, appearing plumper compared to the wild-type (Fig. 1l, m). The length of the epidermal cells in her1 styles decreased while their width increased, making them shorter and wider compared to the wild-type (Fig. 1n, o). These traits indicate that the increased number and thickened size of the stigma brushes in her1 are the primary factors contributing to the increase in stigma volume. Moreover, it can be inferred that the increased total length of the her1 stigma is mainly caused by an increase in the number of longitudinal cells in the style rather than changes in cell morphology.

HER1 encodes a SET domain-containing protein
To determine the inheritance pattern of the mutant traits in her1, we conducted reciprocal crosses between her1 and the wild-type II-32B. The BCF1 plants exhibited the wild-type phenotype regardless of the direction of the cross, and the segregation patterns of two BCF2 populations both followed a 3:1 ratio (Supplementary Table 1), suggesting that the mutant traits of her1 is governed by a single recessive nuclear gene.

We screened 50 extreme mutant-phenotype individuals from the BCF2 population for whole-genome sequencing and MutMap analysis. The SNP-index map showed a significant linkage peak on chromosome 2, containing four SNPs with an SNP-index of 1.0 (Fig. 2a). SNP1 and SNP2 were located in intergenic and promoter regions, respectively. SNP3 and SNP4 fell within coding regions, while SNP4 results in a synonymous mutation, which does not have a functional effect (Supplementary Table 2). SNP3 was located in the coding region of the gene LOC_Os02g47900, named HER1, which was considered the candidate gene controlling the mutant traits. HER1 is comprised of seven exons, and in her1, the 97th base in exon 4 is mutated from A to T, causing a change in the encoded amino acid from arginine (AGA) to a stop codon (TGA) (Fig. 2b). HER1 encodes a SET domain-containing protein, also known as SET Domain Group 706 (SDG706). The mutation in her1 leads to the truncation of the SET domain and complete loss of the post-SET domain (Fig. 2c).

HER1 was constitutively expressed in rice plants, with expression observed in the roots, leaves, panicles, glumes, pistils, and stamens. Its expression level in the pistil was higher than that in other tissues (Supplementary Fig. 3). To validate the biological function of HER1 in regulating stigma size and exsertion, we constructed a CRISPR/Cas9 knockout vector and a functional complementation vector for HER1, which were introduced into the II-32B and her1 backgrounds, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). The phenotypes of the two knockout lines were similar to those of her1, exhibiting significantly increased stigma size and exsertion rate (Fig. 2d–g). Conversely, the phenotypes of the two complementation lines in the her1 background were restored to the wild-type level, with no significant differences in either stigma length or exsertion rate (Fig. 2d–g). These results demonstrate that the traits of her1 are caused by the mutation of HER1, which has a biological function in regulating stigma size and exsertion.

We investigated the biological effects of HER1 in the japonica rice variety Zhonghua 11 (ZH11). The two knockout lines her1-zh-ko1/2 in the ZH11 background showed larger stigmas compared to the wild-type (Supplementary Fig. 5a–c), and the stigma exsertion rate significantly increased from 2.48% to 8.66% and 9.75%, respectively, which is more than a threefold increase compared to the wild-type (Supplementary Fig. 5d). In addition, a ubiquitin promoter-driven overexpression vector of HER1 was constructed and introduced into II-32B (Supplementary Fig. 4c, d). Overexpression of HER1 did not alter the stigma size or exsertion rate in transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 5e–i). Phenotypic variation only occurs when there is a deficiency of HER1.

HER1 specifically binds to methylated histone H3K9 and regulates H3K9me2 levels
SET domain-containing proteins are universally localized in the nucleus and exhibit histone lysine methyltransferase (HKMT) activity37–40. In the covalent modification of histones, HKMTs typically act as writers, establishing methylation marks on various lysine residues of histones, particularly H3 and H4, thereby regulating chromatin conformation and related processes to influence gene expression41. Using BLASTP, proteins with sequence similarity to HER1 were screened in rice and Arabidopsis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that HER1 shares sequence similarity with the H3K9 methyltransferase protein families SUVHs and SUVRs in Arabidopsis, and is highly homologous to the SUVR5, suggesting its potential function in the regulation of H3K9 methylation (Supplementary Fig. 6).

To study the molecular function of HER1 protein, we first transiently expressed a 35S promoter-driven HER1-eGFP fusion protein in onion epidermal cells, and localized HER1 to the nucleus, consistent with a previous report42 (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Immunoblotting analyses were performed using specific antibodies targeting different methylation states of various lysine sites on histone H3 in the stigmas of wild-type and her1. The H3K9me2 level in the stigmas of her1 was reduced by more than 1-fold compared to the wild-type, while the levels of H3K9me1, H3K9me3, and other lysine sites showed minor changes (Fig. 3a). Both knockout and overexpression of HER1 affected the H3K9me2 levels in vivo (Fig. 3b). These results indicate that HER1 protein regulates H3K9me2 levels in plants and may influence the expression of downstream genes through this epigenetic mechanism, thereby modulating stigma exsertion rate in rice.

Using recombinant HER1 in methyltransferase assays, neither western blotting nor mass spectrometry (MS) revealed increased H3K9 methylation compared with controls, and no enzymatic activity was detected when HER1 was further tested using a commercial H3K9 methyltransferase activity kit (ab113453, Abcam) (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 7b–f). All these results are consistent with a previous report42. Therefore, we suggest that HER1 alone may not possess typical HKMT activity but instead interacts with histones through other mechanisms, thereby affecting H3K9me2 levels.

To verify this hypothesis, we performed a GST pull-down assay with GST-HER1 fusion protein, using calf thymus histones or recombinant mononucleosomes as substrates. Calf thymus histones are naturally purified and rich in various covalent modifications, whereas the histones in recombinant mononucleosomes are unmodified. HER1 specifically bound to calf thymus histones but not to recombinant mononucleosomes, suggesting that HER1 may have a preference for specific covalent modifications on histones (Fig. 3d).

We synthesized various biotinylated peptides of histone H3 with different methylation patterns (including H3K4, H3K9, H3K27, H3K36, and unmethylated H3) and performed a peptide pull-down assay using the His-tagged HER1 protein as the substrate. HER1 specifically bound to H3K9me1, H3K9me2, and H3K9me3 peptides but did not bind to H3K4me3, H3K27me3, or H3K36me3 peptides, nor did it bind to unmodified H3 peptides (Fig. 3e). HER1 1-624 protein, expressed using the coding sequence in her1 (Fig. 2c), could not bind to any form of histone H3 peptide (Fig. 3f). To further validate these results, we performed surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis using immobilized GST-HER1 protein. Consistent with the peptide pull-down assay, SPR analysis showed that HER1 selectively bound to H3K9me1, H3K9me2, and H3K9me3 peptides, but not to unmodified H3 peptides or peptides methylated at other lysine residues (Fig. 3g, h and Supplementary Fig. 8a–e). The SPR measurements revealed differences in binding affinities among the H3K9-methylated peptides, with H3K9me2 exhibiting the lowest KD value, suggesting a relatively higher binding affinity compared with the other H3K9-methylated peptides (Supplementary Table 3). In addition, we divided HER1 into three parts, HER1-P1, HER1-P2, and HER1-P3 (P3 contains pre-SET, SET, and post-SET domains), and performed peptide pull-down assays with H3, H3K4me3, H3K9me1/2/3, H3K27me3, and H3K36me3 peptides to test the binding region of the HER1 protein (Supplementary Fig. 8f). Among the three fragments, only HER1-P3, which encompasses the entire SET domain architecture, demonstrated binding affinity to H3K9me peptides, but not to peptides with other modification types (Supplementary Fig. 8g). This finding was further validated using His-tagged constructs (Supplementary Fig. 8h). Based on the observed changes in H3K9me2 levels in her1, as well as in knockout and overexpression lines, it can be inferred that although HER1 may lack HKMT activity, it can specifically bind to H3K9me through P3 (containing SET domain) and maintain its methylation status.

HER1 regulates stigma morphology by modulating the transcription of downstream DS2
Based on the effect of HER1 on histone methylation in vivo (Fig. 3a, b), a Cut&Tag assay was performed using the α-H3K9me2 antibody on stigmas of the wild-type and her1. Global H3K9me2 levels exhibited a notable decline in her1 compared to the wild-type (Fig. 4a), aligning with immunoblotting results (Fig. 3a). Differential analysis on the H3K9me2 peaks identified 550 down-regulated peaks and 255 up-regulated peaks in her1 compared to the wild-type, co-locating with 487 and 236 genes, respectively (Fig. 4b, c). A specific polyclonal antibody, α-HER1, was prepared in rabbits for the identification of downstream targets of the HER1 protein. The Cut&Tag analysis with α-HER1 revealed predominant enrichment of HER1 in the promoter, intergenic, and gene body regions (encompassing CDS and introns), with up to 4559 peaks enriched on the promoters, implying an impact of HER1 on gene transcription (Fig. 4d). Moreover, HER1-enriched peaks exhibited a significant overlap with H3K9me2-enriched peaks in the wild-type, indicating a close relationship between HER1 and di-methylation of H3K9 (Fig. 4e).

RNA-seq analyses on stigmas of II-32B and her1 detected 1542 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with 320 genes down-regulated and 1222 genes up-regulated in her1 compared to the II-32B (Fig. 4f). Considering the repressive effect of H3K9me2 on gene expression34,43–45, we screened genes that were both enriched by HER1 and up-regulated in expression level (in her1), and performed an overlap analysis with genes previously identified in the stigma cell cluster46, identifying five genes as possible downstream targets of HER1 (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Table 4). Principal component analysis (PCA) confirmed the consistency between biological replicates for both Cut&Tag-seq and RNA-seq (Supplementary Fig. 9).

Among these five genes, DS2 (LOC_Os03g02460), which is specifically expressed in stigmas according to the ePlant database47 (https://bar.utoronto.ca/eplant_rice/; Supplementary Fig. 10a), showed significant enrichment of HER1 in both its promoter region and gene body, along with a notable decrease in H3K9me2 levels (Fig. 4h). Chromatin immunoprecipitation quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR) analysis using the α-HER1 antibody further validated the enrichment of HER1 on DS2 gene, and in the her1 mutant, the enrichment of HER1 on DS2 was significantly reduced due to the loss of key binding site of the HER1 protein (Supplementary Fig. 10b, c). Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) was also performed in both II-32B and her1. Unlike the HER1 binding and H3K9me2 enrichment observed at its gene region (Fig. 4h), DS2 exhibited very low DNA methylation in both II-32B and her1 (Supplementary Fig. 10d). Importantly, no appreciable differences in DNA methylation patterns were observed at the DS2 locus between II-32B and her1, despite clear differences in H3K9me2 levels and DS2 expression. These results suggest that HER1 regulates H3K9me2 and DS2 expression in a DNA methylation-independent manner, akin to what has been reported for SUVR5 in Arabidopsis36.

DS2 encodes a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) with an unknown function. The RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high DS2 expression in the stigma, with a significantly increased expression level in the stigma of her1 compared to that of the wild-type (Fig. 4i). Similar to the her1 mutant, two independent DS2 overexpression lines showed significantly enlarged stigmas, with stigma length increased from 1.41 mm to 1.65 mm and 1.68 mm, respectively (Fig. 5a–c). Stigma exsertion rate of both DS2-OE1 and DS-OE2 also significantly increased compared to the wild-type (Fig. 5d). We further knocked out DS2 in both II-32B and her1 to create ds2 single mutant and her1-ds2 double mutant. The ds2 single mutant showed a significant decrease in both stigma length and stigma width compared to II-32B, while loss of function of DS2 in her1 significantly limited the stigma size (Fig. 5e–g). These results further indicated that HER1 regulates the expression of DS2 by modulating H3K9me2 levels, ultimately controlling the stigma size and exsertion (Fig. 5h).

The her1 allele enhances hybrid seed production
The increased exsertion rate observed in the her1 mutant suggests that HER1 may have significant breeding value. We searched for natural mutations of HER1 in 533 rice accessions23 and found 21 variations in HER1 and its promoter region, including 18 SNPs and 3 InDels, with only six mutations located in the coding region (Supplementary Fig. 11a, b). All variations were categorized into six major haplotypes, named Hap1-Hap6, with 137, 108, 75, 72, 69, and 35 accessions included, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 11a). Only the accessions with Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 showed an increase in total stigma length compared to those carrying Hap1, while no significant differences were observed for other haplotypes (Supplementary Fig. 11c). Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 were almost exclusively present in the indica subpopulations (IndI and IndII), whereas Hap1 and Hap6 were predominantly found in the temperate japonica (TeJ) and tropical japonica (TrJ), respectively; Hap5 was more prevalent in TrJ and aus subpopulations, showing minimal presence in indica rice (Supplementary Fig. 11d). To avoid the impacts of genetic background, we compared the phenotypes of accessions carrying Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 in indica groups, while those with Hap1, Hap5, and Hap6 were analyzed in japonica and aus groups. The results showed no significant differences in total stigma length among Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4, nor were there any differences observed among Hap1, Hap5, and Hap6 (Supplementary Fig. 11e, f).

To further analyze the effects of different HER1 haplotypes, we selected three accessions from each of Hap1-Hap4, which had shown statistically significant phenotypic differences, and performed qPCR analysis of the DS2 gene in their stigmas. Among the analyzed accessions, only one accession, W108 (Hap2), showed decreased expression compared to the three specific accessions, C069 (Hap2), W259 (Hap3), and W272 (Hap3), while no significant differences were observed among other accessions (Supplementary Fig. 11g). This differential expression did not show a clear association with the phenotype. Furthermore, we found that the variation explained by haplotypes was less than the variation explained by subpopulations (Supplementary Table 5). Given this lack of correlation between HER1 haplotypes, DS2 expression, and phenotypes, the increased total stigma length observed in accessions with Hap2, Hap3, and Hap4 may be caused by differences in subpopulation genetic architecture, rather than natural variations in HER1. In addition, nucleotide diversity (π) of HER1 and its flanking regions (50 kb upstream and 50 kb downstream) was analyzed in both cultivated rice (Oryza sativa) and wild rice (Oryza rufipogon). The nucleotide diversity value for HER1 is much lower than its flanking regions in both cultivated and wild populations (Oryza rufipogon), suggesting that the minimal natural variation in the locus of HER1 might be the result of natural selection rather than artificial selection (Supplementary Fig. 11h).

Therefore, we introduced the loss-of-function allele from her1 into the sterile line II-32A (matched with II-32B) through backcross breeding, naming the new line herA. Compared to II-32A, herA exhibited enlarged stigma and a significant increase in stigma exsertion rate, rising from 47.48% to 75.42% (Fig. 6a–c). In 2022, we conducted a preliminary outcrossing experiment on herA and II-32A, using II-32B as the pollen donor. Compared to II-32A, the outcrossing rate of herA increased by 23.03%, and the seed production number per plant increased by 19.16% (Supplementary Fig. 12).

We massively propagated the seeds of herA and II-32A and conducted a field seed production trial in 2023. The experimental field was approximately 65.87 m in length and 6.50 m in width, covering an area of about 428.15 m² (Fig. 6d). To ensure uniform pollen distribution, the trial utilized an interplanting method between the sterile (A) and maintainer (B) lines. Each B row was alternated with two A rows, with each A row containing half a row of herA and half a row of II-32A (Fig. 6e, f). The sterile line herA showed a notable increase in seed production per plant compared to II-32A (Fig. 6g). Statistical analyses revealed that the outcrossing rate of herA increased from 40.80% to 50.37% compared to II-32A (an increase of 23.46%), the seed production yield per field plot (10 plants) increased from 124.57 g to 150.46 g (an increase of 20.79%), and the seed production yield per 666.7 m² increased significantly from 175.76 kg to 215.08 kg, showing a substantial increase of 22.37% (Fig. 6h–j).

As a recessive allele, the negative effects of her1 may be masked by the dominant allele from the restorer line in the hybrid rice (F1) generation48. We generated six hybrid rice combinations by crossing the male sterile lines II-32A and herA with three restorer lines, Shuhui12, Shuhui527, and Fuhui838 (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Agronomic trait analysis revealed that the hybrid rice combinations developed using herA and those using II-32A showed no significant differences (P > 0.05) in plant height, panicle number per plant, panicle length, grain number per panicle, seed setting rate, thousand-grain weight, and yield per plant (Supplementary Fig. 13b, h). Final yield of every field plot was tested, and none of them revealed significant differences between the hybrid rice combinations developed using herA and those using II-32A (Supplementary Fig. 13i). These results confirmed the significant practical value of HER1 and provided precious material resources for high-outcrossing sterile line breeding, contributing to hybrid seed production.
